svg.aria-label: The six layers of an embedded Linux board in boot order: the boot ROM in the silicon, first-stage firmware with the secure world (TF-A and OP-TEE), the bootloader (U-Boot or UEFI), the Linux kernel with its device tree, the root filesystem, and the application. Each row says who provides the layer and how often you change it, from never for the boot ROM to daily for the application.
svg.text: Every embedded Linux board is the same stack
Six layers, started in this order. The names change from vendor to vendor; the jobs do not.
Mask ROM inside the SoC. Reads the boot-mode pins or fuses,
finds the first loader on SD, eMMC, QSPI or USB, and runs it.
Starts the DRAM (training), then installs the secure monitor
(TF-A) and optionally a trusted OS (OP-TEE). Stays resident.
U-Boot or UEFI. Picks a kernel and a device tree from storage,
builds the kernel command line, jumps. Then it is gone.
Linux. The device tree (.dtb) tells it which hardware exists
and where; drivers bind to the nodes.
Everything in /: init, shell, libraries, packages, services.
Debian, Alpine, a vendor rootfs, or one you assemble.
The reason the board exists. Runs on top of all of the above
and is the only layer that changes every week.
Boards that flash over USB instead of an SD card (Jetson) swap the last step for NVIDIA's flash tool, but the six layers are the same.
